newsitem.title: USA: Sony needs new script for Hollywood.
newsitem.headline: Sony needs new script for Hollywood.

text.p: When Sony Corp. purchased Columbia Pictures in 1989, many people in Hollywood wondered whether the Japanese electronics company could survive in the rough and tumble world of moviemaking.
Seven years and billions of dollars later, the question is still unanswered.
Now as rumours of another management shakeup swirl around the company's Culver City studio lot, some industry analysts say Sony Entertainment needs a new script.

"They just don't have a business plan that works," said one veteran entertainment analyst who asked not to be identified. "Sony really has to get a business plan at the studio and then put the right people in place to execute the plan.
"They keep looking for someone to bring them a plan and execute it, and every time they turn around they're spending another $500 million."
Seven years ago Sony paid $3.4 billion to acquire Columbia Pictures, and it has spent billions more to upgrade the studio's production facilities.

In the process, it has hired and fired a number of executives, struggling to find the right team to make the investment work. First there was producers Peter Guber and Jon Peters, who were said to have been hired more for their success with the blockbuster "Batman" than their experience running a major studio.

The move proved to be a disaster as the two men spent lavishly on new projects without much success. Shortly after Guber left, the studio took an embarrassing $3.2 billion write-off for its movie-making business, leading many experts to predict the company would soon leave Hollywood.

Thus far, Sony has refused to sell, choosing instead to stick to its original vision that so-called software -- movies, music and television programmes -- and hardware -- compact disc players, VCR's and other machines -- provide an extraordinary combination.

Industry analysts say, however, that recent box office disappointments such as "The Cable Guy," "Multiplicity" and "The Fan" have jeopardised that vision -- not only because they have not provided an adequate financial return in theatres, but also because they leave Sony with fewer assets to exploit down the road when it tries to distribute the products into home video and pay-for-view channels.

Moreover, talent agents fear the constant turmoil in Sony's executive offices is hurting Sony's reputation to the point where many talented writers, directors and actors would rather pitch their ideas to another studio.

A little more than a month ago, Sony tried to quash rumours of an impending house cleaning by issuing an unusual statement in support of Sony Pictures Chairman Alan Levine. But the rumours continued to fly, culminating this week with media reports that the studio was talking with Arnold Rifkin, a top talent agent at William Morris, to replace Columbia TriStar Chairman Mark Canton.
Sony officials declined to comment on the reports, but people familiar with the negotiations say a deal could be announced soon.

Industry analysts say Rifkin, who heads up the motion picture department at William Morris, could help Sony establish important links with the Hollywood community following the summer departures of TriStar President Marc Platt, Columbia Pictures President Lisa Henson and marketing chief Sid Ganis.
But, longer term, Sony needs to find ways to refill its product pipeline and show it can make money.
Unlike rival studios Walt Disney Co. and Time Warner Inc.'s Warner Bros., Sony does not have access to its own broadcast network and therefore must fight harder to get its product into distribution.
Studio executives say the easiest way to do that is to churn out the hits on a regular basis, something Sony Pictures has struggled to do.

At the start of the summer, Sony had high hopes for its new Jim Carrey comedy "Cable Guy", as well as the Michael Keaton film "Multiplicity". But both films did poorly at the box office, earning Sony the dubious distinction of being the only major Hollywood studio without a summer blockbuster.
This fall, the studio will release "Devil's Own" a thriller starring Brad Pitt and Harrison Ford. But Sony will need more than one good film to silence the critics.
